extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in Shakespeare, literary criticism, and theatre history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting interpretive criteria, evaluative standards, and production guidelines found in a Wikipedia article covering criticism, performance history, and adaptations of Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read-as-text versus performed quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The play is often 'best appreciated when read as a text, rather than acted on stage' (Hazlitt, Knight, Gervinus and others argued that reading reveals subtleties lost in performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics who favor reading emphasize textual subtlety, poetic language, and internal coherence; those who stage it must take care not to flatten or misrepresent textual nuances. Example: several 19th-century critics reserve praise for Theseus while urging the play be read rather than performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream/Platonist interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret the play as reflecting Platonism or as a dream: human life is like a dream and the fairy events signal deprived genuine existence (Hermann Ulrici and others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use philosophical frameworks (Plato, dream-as-reality) to account for the play's treatment of illusion vs reality; supporting evidence includes statements about characters' dream-like behaviour and the play's privileging of imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory / ethical construct reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the play as an allegory or ethical construct about the errors of sensual love and moral lessons (G. G. Gervinus viewed it as allegorical depiction of sensual love's errors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map characters and episodes to moral ideas (e.g., fairies as personified dream-gods, lovers' disobedience as lack of filial piety). This approach emphasizes moral didacticism over fantasy or comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody of social stratification / decorum
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether inconsistencies in characters' behaviour (e.g., Theseus and Hippolyta acting like ordinary people, mechanicals aspiring beyond social station) signal a flaw or deliberate parody of class differences (Malone, Ulrici, Halliwell-Phillipps, Charles Knight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue whether breaches of decorum are authorial satire/parody (intentional) or structural weakness; examine stage directions and character behaviour for social coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization depth (especially Bottom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the richness of character-drawing: Bottom is often praised as 'best-drawn' with self-confidence, authority, self-love, and imaginal resources (Knight, Cowden Clarke, others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how convincingly characters embody humanity or types (e.g., Bottom as representative of the human race) and whether their comic traits contribute to thematic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal and function of the fairies
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the fairies as capricious, evanescent beings who may lack intellect/ethics or serve as personified dream-gods (Gervinus, Brandes, Fender, others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether fairies function as moral agents, symbolic forces (unconscious, fertility), or mere supernatural spectacle; this affects readings of agency and responsibility in the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral evaluation of Titania
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate Titania's loyalty and morality (Gervinus views her as immoral for not reconciling, others interpret her actions differently), including whether she deserves punishment or sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use textual evidence of Titania's motives, relationship with Oberon, and narrative consequences to justify moral judgment; note divergent critical stances (punishment vs therapeutic reading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and duration consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the plausibility and consistency of the play's timeframe (Clapp criticized inconsistent time, arguing it detracts; Furness defended the inconsistency as non-detrimental).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether perceived compressions/expansions of time undermine narrative credibility or support thematic/dreamlike effects; staging may clarify or exacerbate temporal ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic/three-phase structural reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the play as a dialectic between realms/stances (Snider's three phases: Real World = reason, Fairy World = imagination/supernatural, Art = self-reflective representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze scene-groupings and shifts of register to demonstrate a structural dialectic; determine whether reconciliation across phases is achieved and how it supports thematic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central themes identification (fantasy, blind love, divine love, metamorphosis, unity, epistemology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how effectively the play explores major themes named by critics (Kermode: fantasy/blind/divine love; Garber: metamorphosis/dream; Berry/Weiner: epistemology and unity; etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support thematic claims by tracing motifs, recurring images (moon, metamorphosis), and argumentative lines of characters (Theseus' speeches); compare to source literature where critics do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexuality, violence, and power dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate readings that emphasize animalistic sexuality, violence, promiscuity, or sadomasochistic aspects of desire (Jan Kott, Richmond, others arguing erotic/sexual readings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine sexual imagery, power relations (Oberon/Titania, lovers in the woods), and textual ambiguity; weigh whether sexuality is central or marginal to the play's comic surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical ambivalence and multiplicity of valid responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge the play's complexity and that characters (Theseus, Hippolyta, Bottom) may have contradictory but partly valid reactions—implying no single authoritative meaning (Stephen Fender).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor readings that allow plural meanings and moral ambivalence rather than forcing a single interpretive closure; consider how staging/production can foreground ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic readings and use of emblematic imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate symbolic interpretations (Zimbardo: Moon phases symbolizing permanence in mutability; discordia concors principle) and how symbols contribute to thematic depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify recurring symbols (moon, changeling, metamorphosis), analyze their semantic range, and show how they support wider interpretive claims about time, change, and reconciliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamorphosis and dream as structuring principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat metamorphosis (entry into woods as dream-like change) as both subject and organizing model of the play; dreams may be prioritized over reason (Marjorie Garber, others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace moments of perception shift, transformations (Bottom's ass-head), and audience/aesthetic effects to argue that dream-logic drives structure and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rites of passage / anthropological communitas reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the woods as a communitas or rite-of-passage space where characters experience release and self-knowledge before returning to social order (Florence Falk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rites-of-passage frameworks to locate stages of development in characters (separation, liminal experience, reintegration) and to justify the play's social-function interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging choices: spectacle versus sparse/innovative production
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate production decisions: Victorian spectacle with large casts, elaborate sets, Mendelssohn music (common in 19th century) versus modern minimalist or innovative stagings (Granville-Barker, Peter Brook's blank white box).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how scale, sets, choreography, and musical accompaniment alter tone and interpretive emphasis; cite historical examples (Madame Vestris' spectacle, Brook's white box) to support claims about staging effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and appropriateness of Mendelssohn and incidental music
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the role of Mendelssohn's overture/incidental music (ubiquitous in 19th-century stagings) and later musical reworkings (Korngold, Orff, Britten) in shaping reception and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss whether Mendelssohn's music complements or colors Shakespeare's text and how alternative musical choices (folk, original scores, modern compositions) affect audience perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubling, casting, and gender/sexuality choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate doubling (e.g., Theseus/Oberon, Hippolyta/Titania), gender-swapping, and queer casting as interpretive strategies that highlight mirrored worlds or modern concerns (Peter Brook, Emma Rice, university queer productions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how casting strategies create thematic resonances (mirroring, fluid identity) and how contemporary reworkings (gender-swapped roles, same-sex couples) update or challenge traditional readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation type and fidelity versus reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the merits of different adaptive formats (operas, ballets, films, rock-opera, disco-theatre) and whether they remain faithful, parodic, or transformative (Purcell, Britten, Balanchine, TV/film adaptations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate adaptations on grounds of fidelity to themes/plot, creative re-imagining, cultural translation, and success within their medium; examples include Purcell's Fairy-Queen, Mendelssohn-based ballets, and film versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spectacle/technology and theatrical gadgets
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the appropriateness and effect of mechanical/technological stage devices (Herbert Beerbohm Tree's mechanical birds, simulated streams, live animals, battery-powered lighting) on the play's comic and fantastic elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether such devices enhance the magical atmosphere or distract from character and theme; historical examples show both extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of the Pyramus and Thisbe play-within-the-play
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the intradiegetic Pyramus and Thisbe episode as parody or pastiche of contemporary theatrical types and as commentary on theatrical representation (Boas: parody of contemporary topos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze its metatheatrical role (comic foil, commentary on acting, parody) and how its staging within productions shapes audience response to both the intradiegetic play and the main plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-based/historicist vs psychological criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose between or balance historicist/source-based interpretations (tracing to Macrobius, Apuleius, Bruno) and psychological/psychoanalytic readings (Puck as unconscious, lovers' sexual development).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical and literary sources to ground thematic claims where appropriate (Kermode), or apply psychological theory to characters' motivations (Aronson, Holland); acknowledge strengths and limits of each method.
